newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Iraq keeps Asian oil price buoyant, but worst over.
newsitem.headline: Iraq keeps Asian oil price buoyant, but worst over.

text.p: Fear of further conflict in the Gulf next week is likely to keep crude prices in Asia buoyant, but oil traders said most of the drama seemed to be over for now.
Benchmark crude oil North Sea Brent prompt futures rose to a post Gulf War high of $23.50 per barrel last week after the United States launched missile strikes against Iraq.
By the end of the week prices had cooled slightly to $22.54 per barrel -- but traders said they would remain wary of the Saddam Hussein factor.
"Everything depends on the aggression factor," said Charles Dobell, managing director from oil brokers GNI in Singapore. "If the Iraqis make another aggression, Brent could rise as high as $25."
Crude prices often rise during times of tension for fear that there could be a major disruption to world oil supplies.
Prices are particularly sensitive to events in the Middle East because the region contains 65 percent of the world's proven oil reserves.

The United States fired 44 missiles on Iraq on Tuesday and Wednesday in retaliation for Iraq's incursion against northern Kurds in the no-fly zone and sent crude oil and petroleum product prices higher.
Brent rose sharply and another benchmark crude oil, the prompt futures contract on the New York Mercantile Exchange (NYMEX) rose to a four-month high of $24.25 per barrel.
But the rally lost steam as the market took the view that most of the drama had finished and that Iraq and the United States were backing away from further confrontation.
"We have to see if there would be further provocation from Saddam Hussein and how the U.S. reacts to it," one crude oil broker said. "The market has reached the top and is now easing off."
But crude oil traders said further Iraqi action would cause another spike in prices.
"Prices could spike higher again if the tension heightens in the Middle East," said James Moonier, executive director of Morgan Stanley Capital Group, in Singapore.
"But if the situation settles down, the prices are expected to calm down as well," he said.
Brent prices could fall to $20 per barrel if traders feel there will be no further conflicts, traders said.
"Unless there is a huge escalation of tension, the prices are expected to drift lower," said Dobell.
He said traders were "more prudent" during the missile attack when compared with the hysteria that surrounded Iraq's invasion of Kuwait in 1990.
But at the same time crude prices are not expected to fall too far during the rest of the year.
The United Nations put on hold the oil-for-food deal with Iraq because of its incursion into the Kurdish region. That has taken supply out of the market.
The deal would have brought 700,000 barrels per day of Iraqi crude back into the market for the first time since the Gulf War. Iraq had been expected to start selling the crude this month.
In addition, low stocks of heating oil and gasoline in the U.S. and low heating oil stocks in Europe are expected to keep refineries busy meeting demand, which will support crude prices.
